summary: David DiNardo reports from week three of building Taxifi in public, three months ahead of its March 2, 2026 launch, and shares the five lessons the first weeks taught him. He explains how EOS quarterly rocks keep him working on the business instead of in it, why he chose creators and sole proprietors as a single vertical, and why an app that does not deliver an outcome will not sell no matter how good the content is.
takeaways: David runs Taxifi on EOS: four to six quarterly rocks per person, anything new goes on the bench for next quarter, and he completed all six Q4 2025 rocks, including launching the website, early access and the corporate structure.
Taxifi's stated vision is a $100 million business valuation within five years, and every website, development and marketing task is worked backwards from that and from the March 2, 2026 launch date.
Niche clarity beats serving everyone: David deliberately speaks only to creators and solopreneurs, and the DMs saying 'you're speaking to me' confirmed that generalist messaging would not land.
People buy outcomes, not apps; Taxifi starts with sole proprietorships because David can automate at least 95% of that process, while incorporations are much harder.
Building in public forces better decisions and generates its own content; documenting the journey means you are never short of things to post.
You cannot automate clarity: David did the problem-definition work in a creative session, not in ChatGPT, because a polished AI answer is not necessarily the right one.
Emotions are data too; as AI outperforms both you and your competitors on the work, your nerves, story and level of vulnerability become the differentiator.
